newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish court opens investigations in Banesto case.
newsitem.headline: Spanish court opens investigations in Banesto case.

text.p: Spain's High Court opened a judicial fraud investigation on Thursday against two associates of disgraced financier Mario Conde, a former chairman of Spanish bank Banesto.
A third businessman Jacques Hachuel, who had dealings with Conde, has been formally charged with fraud in the case. Hachuel was not employed by Banesto.

The court issued an order to investigate Conde's lawyer, Mariano Gomez de Liano, and a business associate, Francisco Sitges, on suspicioun that they ran a network of Swiss companies which diverted funds from Banesto.
Hachuel is alleged to have participated in the operation of a company, Carburos Metalicos, which defrauded Banesto out of 1.3 billion pesetas ($10 million).

Liano is the brother of Javier Gomez de Liano, a prominent high court judge who is trying one of the key cases in Spain's "dirty war" against the Basque separatist group ETA, a campaign by anti-terrorist death squads in which 28 people were killed between 1983 and 1987.
Senior officials of the former Socialist government, including former prime minister Felipe Gonzalez, are suspected of masterminding and funding the death squads.
Sitges is the former chairman of Spanish zinc producer Asturiana de Zinc.

Conde was charged in May with fraud, misappropiation of funds and using false procedures following a 16-month investigation into the 1993 collapse of Banco Espanol de Credito-Banesto, Spain's biggest financial crime case. He is awaiting trial.
Seven other ex-directors were also formally charged in May with fraud relating to the bank's collapse.
The court said then the men were to blame for the crisis at Banesto, which had run up a deficit of 605 billion pesetas ($4.7 billion at current rates of exchange) in 1993.

The judge said there was evidence Conde alone had syphoned off 300 million pesetas from Banesto accounts for personal use. Other ex-bank directors allegedly pocketed money meant to pay suppliers for companies in the Banesto group.
The high court also found fictitious profits were generated by buying and selling holdings via intermediary companies and by revaluing assets.
Banesto was taken over by Banco Santander SA after an auction in April 1994.
